episodes.title: Stop Guessing Your vLLM Config: Benchmarking LLMs on Runpod - Chris Vela, Runpod
episodes.description:
Most teams spin up a new open model with the default vLLM recipe and hope for the best. Runpod forward-deployed engineer Chris Vela shows how to choose configs from data instead, starting with the use case and concurrency, and demos BenchPod, a benchmarking dashboard built on vLLM that tests configs live without restarts. He runs Kimi K3 on a B300, shows how tuning max batch tokens cuts inter-token latency, and asks whether you need a frontier model at all.

episodes.title: Who Is Making This Request? Agent Auth 101 - Kamil Potrec, Keycard
episodes.description:
When an agent sends an invoice using your token, who actually made the request? Kamil Potrec of Keycard breaks down how agents get credentials today (personal tokens, static keys, over-privileged service accounts) and what proper agent auth requires: per-agent identity, delegation, short-lived scoped credentials, federation with legacy systems, policy and audit. He compares SDKs and gateways for keeping credentials out of an agent's reach, including the gateway tradeoffs.

episodes.title: Exploits Now Beat Patches: Open Source Security in the AI Era - Patrick Smyth, Chainguard
episodes.description:
Frontier AI has made every attacker a level more dangerous, and on average, exploits now land before the patch. Patrick Smyth of Chainguard covers this year's AI-assisted attacks and supply chain malware waves, why 30-day remediation windows no longer hold up, the four attack surfaces to cover (malware, known CVEs, zero days and "side doors" like CI/CD, developer laptops and agent skills), and what to do now: cooldown periods, faster CVE fixes, and signing everything with SLSA and Sigstore.

episodes.title: We Kept Rebuilding Our AI Agent. Here's What Survived - Fuad Ali, Arize AI
episodes.description:
Arize's in-product agent Alex went from a 2023 prototype that was "50% hallucination" to a single agent with planning, memory and on-demand skills, all built with custom harness code instead of a framework. AI PM Fuad Ali covers each decision: moving the plan into the harness, making "finish" an explicit gate, treating large tool results like files, why one 8,000-character memory file per user beat vector stores and knowledge graphs, merging 10 specialists into one agent, and using production sessions as tests.

episodes.title: Stop Giving Your Agent Tools. Give It a Sandbox - Mikyo King, Arize AI
episodes.description:
Classic tool-calling agents fill their context with tool catalogs and raw outputs. Code mode gives the agent a sandbox and lets it search for and compose tools in code, returning only what it needs. Mikyo King, head of open source at Arize AI, explains why code mode works, how Arize built it into Phoenix (Bash, a Python sandbox, SQL and even UI control), its hidden costs (secrets, permissions, durability, double sandboxing), and how Harbor evals showed 43% fewer tokens and 31% lower cost.

episodes.title: What a $900M Bank Error Teaches Us About AI Agents - John Feminella, Two Sigma
episodes.description:
In 2020, Citibank accidentally sent about $900 million to Revlon’s lenders instead of an $8 million interest payment, even though the procedure, the warning pop-up and three approvers all did what they were supposed to. John Feminella, who works on AI architecture and engineering at Two Sigma, uses that story to show how to give AI agents real autonomy without locking everything down. He walks through five composable controls: an agent registry, risk-based review, tool access that follows an agent’s declared purpose, shared firm-wide evals, and classifiers that send humans only the approvals that matter. Views are his own, not Two Sigma’s.

episodes.title: Why Are We Still Governing AI Agents Like Software? - Tim Tyler, Gravitee
episodes.description:
Nobody would hire a worker with no ID, no manager and shared passwords, yet that's how most companies deploy AI agents. Tim Tyler of Gravitee presents the Agent Accountability framework, which governs agents like a digital workforce in three stages: Assignment (identity, team, a named human sponsor), Alignment (role, mission and least-privilege authority) and Administration (oversight scorecards, guardian agents and step-by-step recourse when agents go off course).

episodes.title: 300 Agents, 60 People: How We Secured Our Own AI Agents - Aiden Sochowski, Runlayer
episodes.description:
Runlayer is a company of about 60 people running 300+ agents every day. Founding engineer Aiden Sochowski shares what they found once they put a gateway in front of everything and logged every session and tool call: prompt injection through email, PR-review agents getting talked into approvals, over-permissioned bots, one poisoned agent contaminating others, buggy vibe-coded MCP servers burning tokens, and a model switch that raised costs over 100x in a week.

episodes.description:

episodes.title: Agents That Self Improve While You Sleep - Fuad Ali, Arize AI
episodes.description:
In this workshop, Fuad Ali of Arize AI shows how to build a self-improvement loop for AI agents: trace everything, let Signal (an always-on agent) read your traces on a schedule and file deduplicated issues, turn failures into evals and living regression datasets, run experiments to prove a fix works, and keep humans at the highest-leverage points: eval design, dataset curation and reviewing fixes. He demos the loop on a toy-shopping agent with a planted bug and takes questions on evaluating qualitative output, decision models and cost.
